
# How to Make a Video Call: Complete Beginner's Guide


## What is this in plain English?


Remember when the only way to talk face-to-face with someone far away was to physically travel to see them? In the 1970s and 80s, long-distance relationships meant expensive long-distance phone calls (charged by the minute), handwritten letters that took days to arrive, or costly plane tickets for in-person visits. Seeing the face of someone you loved who lived across the country—let alone across the world—meant months of planning and thousands of dollars in travel expenses. Business meetings required flying executives across continents, booking conference rooms, and coordinating schedules days in advance.


Video calling—the ability to see and hear someone in real-time over the internet, from anywhere in the world, for free or nearly free—would have seemed like science fiction to someone in 1980. Today it's so routine that grandparents video chat with grandchildren living in different countries, doctors conduct remote appointments, college students attend classes from their dorm rooms, and job interviews happen without anyone leaving their home. The COVID-19 pandemic made video calling essential overnight, pushing millions who'd never used it before to learn quickly.


Yet despite how common video calling has become, many people—especially those who didn't grow up with this technology—find it intimidating. There's anxiety about the technology not working, about appearing awkward on camera, about not knowing which buttons to press, about accidentally showing something you didn't mean to show, or about looking foolish in front of others. These fears are completely understandable and completely solvable with clear, patient instruction.


This guide teaches you everything: understanding what video calling is and what you need, choosing which video call service to use (Zoom, FaceTime, Google Meet, Skype, WhatsApp), making your first video call step-by-step, joining video calls others send you, understanding the interface (mute, camera on/off, screen sharing), solving common technical problems, looking and sounding your best on camera, staying safe and private during video calls, and troubleshooting when things don't work. Whether you want to video chat with family, attend a remote doctor's appointment, join a virtual meeting, or take an online class, this guide walks you through everything with patience and clarity.


By the end, video calling will feel natural and accessible—not intimidating or mysterious—and you'll have the confidence to connect with anyone, anywhere, at any time.


## Before You Start: Understanding Video Calls


**What is a Video Call?**


A video call (also called video chat, video conference, or video meeting) is a live conversation where you can see and hear the other person(s) through your computer, phone, or tablet screen—and they can see and hear you—using an internet connection.


**How it works:**

1. Your device's camera captures your video
2. Your device's microphone captures your audio
3. This information travels through the internet to the other person's device
4. Their video and audio travel back to you
5. Both of you see and hear each other in real-time (with slight delay of a fraction of a second)

**Video call vs. phone call:**

- **Phone call:** Audio only, uses phone network
- **Video call:** Audio + video, uses internet (WiFi or cellular data)

**Video call vs. video message:**

- **Video call:** Live, real-time—both people must be present simultaneously
- **Video message:** Recorded video sent like a text—watch whenever convenient

**What You Need for Video Calls:**


**Essential:**


**1. Device with camera and microphone:**

- **Computer:** Most laptops have built-in webcam and microphone (usually at top of screen)
- **Smartphone:** iPhone or Android (front and rear cameras, built-in microphone)
- **Tablet:** iPad or Android tablet (front and rear cameras, built-in microphone)

**Check if your device has a camera:**

- **Windows:** Press Windows key, type "Camera," open Camera app—does it show your face?
- **Mac:** Open Photo Booth app (Applications → Photo Booth)—does it show your face?
- **iPhone/iPad:** Open Camera app, tap flip icon—does front camera show your face?

**2. Internet connection:**

- **WiFi:** Home internet, coffee shop, library
- **Cellular data:** 4G/5G (uses data plan—can be expensive for long calls)
- **Speed requirement:** Minimum 1-2 Mbps (megabits per second) for one-on-one video calls, 3-4 Mbps for group calls
- **Check speed:** Visit speedtest.net on your device

**3. Video calling app or service:**

- Software that enables video calls
- Many options (covered in Step 1)
- Most are free for personal use

**Helpful but optional:**


**4. Headphones or earbuds:**

- Reduces echo (your speakers feeding back into your microphone)
- Improves audio quality for you and others
- Privacy (others in room can't hear both sides of conversation)
- Not essential for most calls but improves experience

**5. External webcam (for computers):**

- Better video quality than built-in laptop webcam
- Adjustable positioning
- Only needed if built-in camera is poor quality or broken

**6. External microphone:**

- Clearer audio than built-in microphone
- Only needed for professional use or if built-in microphone poor

**Most people need only their existing device and internet connection—you likely have everything already.**


**Types of Video Calls:**


**One-on-one (person-to-person):**

- You + one other person
- Simplest, most common (calling family member, friend, doctor)
- Like traditional phone call but with video

**Group call:**

- Three or more people
- Family gatherings, friends catching up, small meetings
- Everyone sees everyone (or multiple faces on screen)

**Large meeting/webinar:**

- 10-100+ people
- Work meetings, online classes, presentations
- Usually one or few people speaking, others listening/watching
- May have features like "raise hand," chat, screen sharing

**Understanding Video Call Services:**


Many different companies offer video calling—they're all similar but with slight differences. You don't need all of them; one or two will cover most people's needs.


**Quick comparison:**


| Service                | Best For                     | Device                  | Free?                            | Notes                                        |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| **FaceTime**           | Apple device users           | iPhone, iPad, Mac only  | Yes                              | Easy, high quality, but Apple-only           |
| **WhatsApp**           | International family/friends | Phone, tablet, computer | Yes                              | Very popular worldwide, works cross-platform |
| **Zoom**               | Meetings, classes, groups    | Computer, phone, tablet | Yes (40-min limit for 3+ people) | Most popular for work/education              |
| **Google Meet**        | Gmail users, simple calls    | Computer, phone, tablet | Yes                              | Easy if you have Gmail account               |
| **Skype**              | Traditional video calling    | Computer, phone, tablet | Yes                              | Older service, still works well              |
| **Facebook Messenger** | Facebook friends             | Phone, tablet, computer | Yes                              | If you're already on Facebook                |


**You'll learn more about choosing in Step 1.**


**Common Video Call Fears (Addressed):**


**"I'll accidentally do something wrong and break it"**

- Reality: You can't break anything. Worst case: Call disconnects and you reconnect
- Buttons are clearly labeled
- Can always end call and try again

**"I'll look bad or awkward on camera"**

- Reality: Everyone feels this at first; it passes with practice
- Other person is focused on talking with you, not judging appearance
- Simple tips (covered later) make huge difference

**"The technology won't work"**

- Reality: Usually works smoothly, and when it doesn't, solutions are simple
- Most problems: internet connection, muted microphone, camera off
- This guide covers troubleshooting

**"I'll accidentally show something I don't want to show"**

- Reality: Camera shows only what's directly in front of it (your face, and background behind you)
- You control when camera is on or off
- Can preview yourself before others see you

**"It's too complicated for someone my age"**

- Reality: Millions of people in their 70s, 80s, and 90s video call regularly
- If you can make a phone call, you can make a video call (actually easier—you see who you're calling)
- With patient instruction, anyone can learn

## Step 1: Choosing Your Video Call Service


**You don't need to choose just one—many people use 2-3 different services for different purposes.** But starting with one makes learning easier.


**Choose Based on Your Situation:**


**Scenario 1: Video calling family members who use iPhones or Macs**
→ **Use FaceTime** (built-in, zero setup, excellent quality, Apple-only)


**Scenario 2: Video calling family or friends internationally**
→ **Use WhatsApp** (free international calls, works on all devices, widely used worldwide)


**Scenario 3: Attending work meetings, online classes, or large group calls**
→ **Use Zoom** (most common for meetings/education, handles large groups well)


**Scenario 4: You use Gmail and want something simple**
→ **Use Google Meet** (integrated with Gmail, easy for Gmail users)


**Scenario 5: General video calling with anyone**
→ **Use Skype** or **WhatsApp** (both work with anyone on any device)


**Scenario 6: Video calling Facebook friends**
→ **Use Facebook Messenger** (if you're already comfortable with Facebook)


**Still unsure? Default recommendations:**

- **iPhone/iPad/Mac user:** Start with FaceTime (already installed)
- **Android/Windows user:** Start with WhatsApp or Google Meet
- **For joining meetings others schedule:** Install Zoom (most common for meetings)

**Installing the Service (If Needed):**


**FaceTime:**

- **iPhone/iPad:** Pre-installed (purple icon with white video camera)
- **Mac:** Pre-installed (Applications → FaceTime)
- **Windows/Android:** Not available (use alternative)

**WhatsApp:**

- **iPhone:** App Store → Search "WhatsApp" → Install
- **Android:** Google Play Store → Search "WhatsApp" → Install
- **Computer:** Visit whatsapp.com → Download for Mac/Windows

**Zoom:**

- **iPhone/Android:** App Store/Play Store → Search "Zoom Cloud Meetings" → Install
- **Computer:** Visit zoom.us → Download → Zoom Client for Meetings
- **OR:** Join via web browser without installing (most browsers support this)

**Google Meet:**

- **No installation needed on computer:** Visit meet.google.com in browser
- **iPhone/Android:** App Store/Play Store → Search "Google Meet" → Install (optional—can use browser)

**Skype:**

- **All devices:** Visit skype.com → Download for your device
- **OR:** Use web.skype.com in browser

**Creating an Account (If Needed):**


**No account needed:**

- FaceTime (uses Apple ID you already have)
- Google Meet (uses Gmail account you already have)
- Zoom (can join meetings without account; need account to host)

**Account required:**

- WhatsApp (uses your phone number)
- Skype (Microsoft account)

**Account setup is simple:**

- Provide email address and create password
- Verify email
- Add phone number (sometimes)
- Usually takes 2-3 minutes

## Step 2: Making Your First Video Call (Step-by-Step)


**We'll cover the most common services. The process is similar across all—learn one, others are easy.**


**FaceTime (iPhone/iPad/Mac):**


**On iPhone/iPad:**

1. **Open FaceTime app** (purple icon with white video camera)
2. **Tap the + button** (top-right corner, or center if no recent calls)
3. **Enter person's name, phone number, or email:**
    - If they're in your contacts: Type their name, tap when it appears
    - If not in contacts: Type their phone number or email address
4. **Tap "FaceTime"** button (shows video camera icon)
5. **Wait for them to answer:**
    - Your camera activates (you see yourself while waiting)
    - Ringing sound plays
    - When they answer, you see them (they see you)
6. **During the call:**
    - Their face fills the screen
    - Your face in small window (usually top corner—can drag to move)
    - Buttons at bottom (covered in Step 3)
7. **End call:**
    - Tap red phone icon (end call button)

**On Mac:**

1. **Open FaceTime** (Applications → FaceTime, or Spotlight search)
2. **Click "New FaceTime"** button
3. **Type name, phone number, or email** in "To:" field
4. **Click video camera icon** OR press Enter
5. **Wait for answer** → Call begins when they answer
6. **End call:** Click red X button (end call)

**WhatsApp:**


**Setup first (one-time):**

1. Open WhatsApp
2. Agree to terms
3. Enter phone number
4. Verify with code sent via SMS
5. Set profile name (your name)

**Making a video call:**

1. **Open WhatsApp**
2. **Tap Calls tab** (bottom of screen, phone icon)
3. **Tap + button** (top-right) OR **call icon** (top-right)
4. **Select contact** from list
    - OR: Tap search, enter name/number
5. **Tap video camera icon** next to their name
6. **Wait for answer** → Call connects
7. **During call:** Face fills screen, controls at bottom
8. **End call:** Tap red phone icon

**Alternative method (from chat):**

1. Open WhatsApp
2. Tap Chats tab
3. Tap conversation with person you want to call
4. Tap video camera icon (top-right)
5. Call begins

**Zoom (Starting a Meeting):**


**To call one person or start a meeting:**

1. **Open Zoom app** OR go to zoom.us and sign in
2. **Click "New Meeting"** button (orange button)
3. **Your video preview appears:**
    - Check how you look
    - Adjust camera angle if needed
    - Click "Join with Video" (green button)
4. **You enter the meeting room:**
    - Your video shows on screen
    - You're alone (others haven't joined yet)
5. **Invite the person:**
    - Click "Participants" button (bottom toolbar)
    - Click "Invite" button
    - Choose method:
        - **Copy invitation link** → paste in text or email to person
        - **Email** → sends invitation via email app
        - **Send link via message/text**
6. **They click the link** → Join your meeting
7. **Their video appears** when they join
8. **End meeting:** Click red "End" button → "End Meeting for All"

**Google Meet:**


**On computer:**

1. **Visit meet.google.com** in browser (Chrome recommended)
2. **Sign in** with Gmail account (if not already)
3. **Click "New meeting"** button
4. **Choose:**
    - **Start an instant meeting:** Begins immediately, you get link to share
    - **Create a meeting for later:** Schedule for future time
    - **Schedule in Google Calendar:** Opens calendar to schedule
5. **For instant meeting:**
    - Meeting starts
    - Your video appears
    - Copy meeting link (shown at top)
    - Send link to person via text, email, or message
    - They click link → Join your meeting
6. **End meeting:** Click red phone icon

**On phone (Google Meet app):**

1. **Open Google Meet app**
2. **Tap "New"** button (bottom-right)
3. **Choose "Start an instant meeting"**
4. **Tap "Join now"**
5. **Tap "Share invite"** → Send link via text or email
6. **Recipient clicks link** → Joins call

**Skype:**

1. **Open Skype app** or visit web.skype.com
2. **Click "New" button** (top-left, + symbol)
3. **Select "New Call"**
4. **Search for contact:**
    - Type their name (if they're on Skype)
    - OR: Enter phone number (Skype can call regular phones for a fee)
5. **Click their name** when it appears
6. **Click video camera icon** to start video call
7. **Wait for answer** → Call begins
8. **End call:** Click red phone icon

## Step 3: Joining a Video Call Someone Else Started


**This is even easier than starting your own call—someone sends you a link or invites you, you click it, you're in.**


**Joining a Zoom Meeting:**


**Someone sent you a Zoom link** (looks like: zoom.us/j/1234567890 or a "Join Zoom Meeting" button in email)

1. **Click the link** (in email, text message, or wherever they sent it)
2. **Browser opens Zoom** OR prompts to open Zoom app
    - If prompted: Click "Open Zoom" or "Launch Meeting"
    - If using browser: May join directly in browser
3. **Enter your name** when prompted (how you'll appear to others)
4. **Video preview appears:**
    - You see yourself
    - Check appearance
    - Can adjust camera angle
5. **Click "Join with Video"** (or "Join Meeting")
    - If you don't want video on: Click "Join without Video"
6. **You enter the meeting:**
    - May see waiting room message ("Waiting for host to let you in")
    - Host admits you → You see other participants

**Troubleshooting Zoom join issues:**

- **Zoom app not installed:** Download from zoom.us first, then click link again
- **Meeting hasn't started:** Message says "Meeting not started"—wait or contact person who invited you
- **Wrong meeting ID:** Double-check link or meeting ID number

**Joining Google Meet:**


**Someone sent you a Google Meet link** (looks like: meet.google.com/abc-defg-hij)

1. **Click the link**
2. **Browser opens Google Meet**
3. **Sign in** with Google/Gmail account (if not already)
    - Can join without account (click "Join as guest," enter name)
4. **Video and audio preview:**
    - Adjust camera, check appearance
    - Test microphone
5. **Click "Ask to join"** button
6. **Host admits you** → You enter meeting

**Joining via Google Calendar invitation:**

- If meeting scheduled via Google Calendar
- Calendar event has "Join with Google Meet" button
- Click button → Joins meeting directly

**Joining WhatsApp Video Call:**


**Someone calls you via WhatsApp:**

1. **WhatsApp rings** (just like a phone call)
2. **Notification shows:** "WhatsApp Video Call from [Name]"
3. **Swipe to answer** (phone) OR **click "Answer"** (computer)
4. **Call connects** → You see them, they see you

**During call:** Same controls as making call yourself


**Joining FaceTime Call:**


**Someone calls you via FaceTime:**

1. **iPhone/iPad rings** (or Mac notification appears)
2. **Notification shows:** "FaceTime Video - [Name]"
3. **Swipe to answer** (iPhone) OR **click "Accept"** (Mac)
4. **Call begins**

**FaceTime link (iOS 15+ and Mac):**

- Someone may send FaceTime link via text/email
- Click link → Opens FaceTime app → Join call
- Android/Windows users: Opens in browser (FaceTime now works in browser for join-only)

**Joining Skype Call:**


**Someone calls you via Skype:**

1. **Skype rings** (audio alert, visual notification)
2. **Notification shows:** "Video call from [Name]"
3. **Click green video camera icon** (answer with video)
    - OR: Click phone icon (answer with audio only)
4. **Call connects**

**Skype link:**

- Someone may send "Join Skype Meeting" link
- Click link → Opens Skype OR browser → Join meeting

## Step 4: Understanding the Video Call Interface


**During any video call, you'll see similar controls. Knowing what each button does removes anxiety.**


**Common Buttons and What They Do:**


**Mute button (microphone icon):**

- **What it does:** Turns your microphone on or off
- **When to use:** Mute when you're not speaking (reduces background noise for others)
- **Visual indicator:** Microphone icon usually shows slash through it when muted
- **Shortcut (Zoom):** Spacebar to temporarily unmute while holding

**Camera on/off button (video camera icon):**

- **What it does:** Turns your camera on or off
- **When off:** Others see black screen or your profile picture instead of your face
- **When to use:** Turn off when you need privacy, when connection is slow, or when eating/drinking
- **Your audio continues** even when video is off

**End call button (red phone icon):**

- **What it does:** Ends the call immediately
- **Usually:** Bottom center or top corner of screen
- **Confirmation:** Some services ask "Are you sure?" before ending

**Flip camera (phone/tablet only):**

- **What it does:** Switches between front camera (facing you) and rear camera (facing away)
- **When to use:** Show something in your environment, show view out window, etc.
- **Icon:** Usually circular arrows or camera with arrows

**Speaker/audio settings:**

- **What it does:** Adjusts speaker volume, chooses audio output device
- **On computer:** Can select headphones vs. speakers
- **On phone:** Adjusts call volume

**Participants/people button:**

- **What it does:** Shows list of who's in the call
- **Useful for:** Seeing who's joined, how many people present (in group calls)

**Chat button:**

- **What it does:** Opens text chat alongside video
- **When to use:** Send links, type something without interrupting speaker, ask questions in large meetings
- **Messages visible to:** Everyone in call (usually—check settings)

**Screen share button:**

- **What it does:** Shows your computer/phone screen to others
- **When to use:** Showing a document, presentation, photos, website
- **How to use:** Click button → Select which screen/window to share → Click "Share"
- **Stop sharing:** Click "Stop Share" button

**Gallery/speaker view toggle:**

- **Gallery view:** Shows all participants equally sized (tiles)
- **Speaker view:** Shows active speaker large, others small
- **Toggle between:** Click view button (Zoom: top-right corner)

**Settings/more options (three dots ⋮ or gear icon ⚙):**

- **What it does:** Opens advanced settings
- **Contains:** Video settings, audio settings, virtual backgrounds, effects

**Raise hand (in meetings):**

- **What it does:** Signals you have something to say without interrupting
- **Host sees:** Notification, hand icon next to your name
- **When to use:** Large meetings, classes (polite way to get attention)

**Reactions (emoji):**

- **What it does:** Send emoji reaction (👍, ❤️, 😂, 👏)
- **Appears:** Briefly on screen, visible to everyone
- **When to use:** Express agreement, appreciation without unmuting

**Leave/end meeting distinction (for hosts):**

- **Leave meeting:** You exit but meeting continues for others
- **End meeting for all:** Closes meeting for everyone (only host can do this)

## Step 5: Looking and Sounding Your Best


**You don't need expensive equipment. Small adjustments make huge differences.**


**Camera Position and Angle:**


**Height:**

- **Camera at eye level** or slightly above (most flattering)
- Not below (looking up at you—unflattering, shows ceiling)
- **Laptop users:** Elevate laptop with books or laptop stand
- **Phone/tablet users:** Prop against something or use stand

**Distance:**

- **Arm's length away** (about 2-3 feet)
- Too close: Face fills entire screen awkwardly
- Too far: You're a tiny person in large frame, hard to see
- **Frame your head and shoulders** (like a passport photo)

**Center yourself:**

- Your face should be **center of frame**
- Not off to one side or top corner
- **Rule of thirds:** Eyes roughly in top third of frame

**Lighting:**


**The most important factor in video quality—matters far more than expensive cameras.**


**Face the light source:**

- **Window light (best natural option):** Sit facing window, light on your face
- **Lamp light:** Place lamp in front of you (not behind)
- **Overhead light:** Better than nothing but creates shadows under eyes

**Avoid backlighting:**

- Don't sit with window or bright light behind you
- Creates silhouette effect (you appear dark, background bright)
- Camera exposes for bright background, making your face dark

**Simple lighting improvement:**

- **Desk lamp** in front of you, angled at your face
- **Two lamps** (left and right sides) even better (reduces shadows)
- **Ring light** ($20-40) excellent affordable option for frequent video calls

**Lighting tips:**

- Soft, diffused light better than harsh direct light
- Natural daylight (cloudy day) incredibly flattering
- Avoid colored lights (warm yellow, cool blue change skin tone)

**Background:**


**What's behind you matters—people notice.**


**Ideal backgrounds:**

- Plain wall (solid color)
- Bookshelf (shows personality, not too cluttered)
- Clean, tidy room
- Nature view through window (but ensure light still on your face)

**Avoid backgrounds:**

- Unmade bed (looks unprofessional)
- Messy room (distracting)
- Bright window behind you (backlighting problem)
- Inappropriate posters or items

**Quick fixes:**

- **Rearrange:** Shift your position so camera sees better background
- **Tidy quickly:** Move clutter out of frame
- **Virtual background:** Zoom, Teams, Google Meet offer digital backgrounds (replaces your real background—can look artificial but useful in pinch)

**Using virtual backgrounds:**

- Settings/effects → Virtual backgrounds
- Choose preset (office, nature, abstract) or upload your own
- Works best with plain background behind you (for clean separation)
- **Green screen** (optional—$15-30) improves virtual background quality

**Audio Quality:**


**Clear audio matters more than perfect video.** People tolerate grainy video but won't tolerate inaudible audio.


**Microphone tips:**


**Reduce background noise:**

- Close windows (traffic, construction)
- Turn off fans, heaters, air conditioners
- Quiet environment (tell others you're on a call)
- Mute when not speaking (removes ambient noise for others)

**Speak clearly toward microphone:**

- **Built-in laptop mic:** Speak directly toward laptop (usually mic near webcam)
- **Phone mic:** Hold phone naturally, don't cover mic with hand
- **Earbuds/headphones with mic:** Mic usually near mouth already (good audio automatically)

**Headphones reduce echo:**

- Echo happens when your speakers feed back into your mic
- Headphones prevent this (audio goes into your ears, not room)
- Any headphones/earbuds work (don't need expensive ones)

**Test your audio:**

- Before important call: Call a friend or family member as test
- Check "can you hear me clearly?"
- Adjust as needed

**Check internet connection:**


**Poor connection causes:**

- Frozen video
- Choppy, robotic audio
- Dropped calls

**Improve connection:**

- **Use WiFi instead of cellular data** when possible (more stable, faster)
- **Sit closer to WiFi router** (better signal)
- **Close other internet-using apps/programs** (stops bandwidth competition)
- **Ask others in house to pause streaming** during important call
- **Restart router** if connection seems slow
- **Use wired Ethernet connection** if available (most stable—computer only)

**Clothing and Appearance:**


**Dress as you would for in-person interaction:**

- Doctor appointment: Business casual
- Family video chat: Whatever you'd wear at home
- Job interview: Professional attire (yes, even on video)

**Clothing tips:**

- **Avoid very fine patterns** (stripes, small checks)—causes moiré effect (weird shimmering on camera)
- **Solid colors** work best
- **Avoid white** against white wall (you blend in)
- **Contrast with background** (dark shirt if light background, light shirt if dark background)

**Grooming:**

- Style hair as normal
- Camera adds slight weight—doesn't matter, everyone experiences same effect
- Makeup (if you wear it): Slightly more than usual compensates for video flattening effect

**Looking at Camera vs. Screen:**


**Natural instinct:** Look at person's face on screen
**Problem:** To them, you appear to be looking down (you're looking at screen, not camera)


**Solution:** Look at camera (the tiny dot at top of screen) when speaking

- Feels weird initially (like talking to a dot)
- To listener: Feels like you're making eye contact
- **Practice:** Look at camera when speaking, glance at screen to see their reactions

**Balance:** Alternate between looking at camera and screen—doesn't need to be perfect


## Step 6: Video Call Etiquette


**Unwritten rules that make video calls pleasant for everyone.**


**Before the Call:**


**Test your tech:**

- 5 minutes before important call, test camera and microphone
- Join early for meetings (5 minutes before start)
- Ensure device is charged (or plugged in)

**Prepare your space:**

- Tidy visible background
- Close irrelevant browser tabs/programs (if screen sharing)
- Silence phone notifications
- Alert others in household you'll be on a call

**Join on time:**

- Punctuality matters as much as in-person
- For meetings: Join 2-3 minutes early
- For casual calls: Call at agreed time

**During the Call:**


**Mute when not speaking (group calls especially):**

- Background noise (dogs barking, kids playing, keyboard typing) distracts everyone
- Unmute when it's your turn to speak
- **Shortcut:** Spacebar to temporarily unmute (Zoom)

**Avoid multitasking:**

- Don't check email, browse web, or do other work during call
- Others can tell you're distracted
- Disrespectful to speaker

**Stay in frame:**

- Don't wander off-camera mid-sentence
- If you need to leave briefly, say "excuse me for a moment" and mute/turn off camera

**Minimize distractions:**

- Eating/drinking on camera acceptable casually (with family) but avoid in professional calls
- If you must eat, mute and turn camera off
- Smoking: Turn camera off (or don't smoke during call)

**Let others finish speaking:**

- Interruptions worse on video than in-person (audio lag means you talk over each other)
- Wait an extra half-second before speaking after someone finishes

**Use chat appropriately:**

- Relevant links, questions, comments: Good
- Side conversations during meeting: Distracting
- Assume host can see all chat (usually they can)

**In Larger Meetings:**


**Raise hand feature:**

- Use virtual "raise hand" instead of interrupting
- Host calls on you when it's your turn

**Stay muted until called on:**

- Unmute only when speaking
- Prevents accidental noise from disrupting

**Rename yourself (if needed):**

- Some platforms show your name incorrectly
- Participants → Click your name → Rename
- Use real name for professional meetings

**Ending the Call:**


**Say goodbye:**

- Don't just click "end" abruptly
- "Thanks for the call, talk to you soon!"
- Wait for other person to say goodbye too

**Let host end meeting (large meetings):**

- Participants leave first, host ends last
- Ensures everyone said what they needed to

**Follow up:**

- Send any promised information afterward
- Thank you message appropriate for professional calls

## Step 7: Troubleshooting Common Problems


**Problem 1: "They can't hear me" / "My microphone isn't working"**


**Check microphone isn't muted:**

- Look for **microphone icon with slash** through it (muted)
- Click to unmute

**Check device volume:**

- Is your device volume turned up?
- Hardware volume buttons (side of phone/laptop)
- System settings → Sound → Input volume slider

**Check app permissions:**

- App may not have permission to use microphone
- **iPhone:** Settings → Privacy → Microphone → [App name] → Toggle ON
- **Android:** Settings → Apps → [App name] → Permissions → Microphone → Allow
- **Mac:** System Preferences → Security & Privacy → Privacy → Microphone → Check app
- **Windows:** Settings → Privacy → Microphone → Allow apps to access → Toggle ON

**Check correct microphone selected:**

- If using external microphone or headset
- Settings → Audio → Microphone → Select correct device from dropdown
- Test each option until sound works

**Restart app:**

- Close app completely
- Reopen and rejoin call

---


**Problem 2: "They can't see me" / "My camera isn't working"**


**Check camera isn't turned off:**

- Look for **video icon with slash** (camera off)
- Click to turn on

**Check app permissions:**

- Same process as microphone permissions above
- **iPhone:** Settings → Privacy → Camera → [App name] → Toggle ON
- **Android:** Settings → Apps → [App name] → Permissions → Camera → Allow
- **Mac:** System Preferences → Security & Privacy → Privacy → Camera → Check app
- **Windows:** Settings → Privacy → Camera → Allow apps to access → Toggle ON

**Check another app isn't using camera:**

- Only one app can use camera at a time
- Close other apps that use camera (Skype, Zoom, Camera app)
- Rejoin video call

**Check camera isn't covered:**

- Laptop cameras often have physical privacy slider/cover
- Slide it open
- Remove any tape or sticker covering camera

**Restart device:**

- Close all apps
- Restart computer/phone
- Try again

---


**Problem 3: "Video is frozen or choppy"**


**Check internet connection:**

- Visit speedtest.net → Run speed test
- Need minimum 1-2 Mbps for video calls
- If slow: Move closer to WiFi router, disconnect other devices, pause downloads

**Turn off your video temporarily:**

- Audio continues, video turns off
- Reduces bandwidth requirements
- Useful when connection struggles

**Ask others to turn off their video:**

- In group calls, multiple video streams use lots of bandwidth
- Everyone turns off video except current speaker

**Close other programs:**

- Streaming video, downloads, large file uploads use bandwidth
- Close these during video calls

**Restart router:**

- Unplug router for 30 seconds
- Plug back in, wait for full restart (2-3 minutes)
- Rejoin call

---


**Problem 4: "There's an echo"**


**Someone's speakers feeding into their microphone:**

- Usually happens when someone uses speakers instead of headphones
- Solution: Everyone uses headphones/earbuds

**Mute when not speaking:**

- Reduces echo for others
- Unmute only when you're talking

**Turn down speaker volume:**

- Quieter speakers less likely to echo into microphone

---


**Problem 5: "I can't join the meeting" / "Invalid meeting ID"**


**Double-check the link:**

- Copy and paste entire link (don't type manually)
- Ensure link didn't break across lines in email

**Meeting hasn't started:**

- Host must start meeting before you can join
- Wait or contact person who invited you

**Meeting already ended:**

- Some meetings have time limits
- Contact host to restart or send new link

**Zoom app not installed:**

- Download Zoom app from zoom.us
- Click link again after installing

**Try joining in web browser:**

- Instead of app, join via browser
- Click link → Click "Join from Your Browser"

---


**Problem 6: "Video call is using too much data" (phone)**


**Data warning on cellular:**

- Video calls use lots of cellular data
- Solution: Use WiFi whenever possible
- Settings → disable cellular data for video call apps (force WiFi-only use)

**Reduce video quality:**

- Some apps let you lower video quality (Zoom: Settings → Video → Enable HD off)
- Uses less data

**Turn off video:**

- Audio-only calls use far less data
- Keep camera off, audio still works

**Problem 7: "Background is distracting/messy"**


**Use virtual background:**

- Zoom, Teams, Google Meet → Settings → Virtual backgrounds
- Replaces real background digitally

**Blur background:**

- Many services offer background blur (less extreme than virtual background)
- Settings → Video → Background effects → Blur

**Reposition camera:**

- Point camera at plain wall instead of messy room

---


**Problem 8: "Audio and video don't sync"**


**Caused by poor internet connection:**

- Close bandwidth-heavy apps
- Move closer to router
- Restart router

**Caused by processing power:**

- Close unnecessary programs on computer
- Older devices may struggle with video processing

**Ask participants to rejoin:**

- Sometimes fixes sync issues

---


**Problem 9: "Someone's background noise is disruptive"**


**Politely ask them to mute:**

- "Hey [name], can you mute when you're not speaking? We're hearing background noise."
- In professional meetings, host should ask

**Host can mute participants:**

- Most platforms let host mute someone remotely
- Participants → Click person's name → Mute

**Enable noise cancellation:**

- Some apps have AI noise cancellation
- Settings → Audio → Noise suppression or background noise reduction

---


**Problem 10: "I don't know which app to use"**


**If someone invited you:**

- They'll specify (Zoom, Google Meet, FaceTime, etc.)
- Click the link they sent—usually opens correct app automatically

**If you're initiating:**

- Use whichever app the other person already has
- Ask them: "Do you have Zoom/FaceTime/WhatsApp?"
- Use that one (easiest for both)

## Step 8: Security and Privacy


**Video calls are generally safe, but simple precautions protect your privacy.**


**Protecting Your Privacy:**


**Be aware of what's visible:**

- **Camera shows everything in frame:** Background, items on walls, people walking by
- Preview yourself before call starts
- Remove or move anything you don't want others seeing

**Use waiting room feature:**

- Zoom and Teams have waiting rooms
- Host admits each person individually
- Prevents uninvited people from joining

**Don't share meeting links publicly:**

- Social media, public forums: Anyone can join
- Send links only to intended participants via email or text

**Password-protect meetings:**

- Zoom, Google Meet, Teams allow password-protected meetings
- When creating meeting, enable password
- Only people with password can join

**Check who's in the meeting:**

- Before sharing sensitive info, check participants list
- Remove any unexpected/unknown participants

**Screen Sharing Safety:**


**Before sharing screen:**

- Close windows/tabs you don't want others seeing
- Email, bank websites, personal photos
- Minimize or close everything except what you're presenting

**Share specific window instead of entire screen:**

- Zoom → Screen Share → "Choose Window" instead of "Entire Screen"
- Shows only that program, not desktop or other windows

**Stop sharing when finished:**

- Click "Stop Share" immediately
- Prevents accidentally showing private info later

**Turn off notifications:**

- Mac: Hold Option, click notification center icon (top-right) → Do Not Disturb
- Windows: Settings → System → Focus assist → On
- Prevents notifications from appearing on shared screen

**Scams and "Zoom-bombing":**


**"Zoom-bombing" (rare but can happen):**

- Uninvited people join meeting and disrupt (offensive content, harassment)
- Prevention: Password-protect meetings, use waiting room, don't share links publicly

**Phishing emails about meetings:**

- Fake emails claiming "you missed a meeting, click here"
- Links lead to malware or fake sites
- Verify with sender before clicking unexpected meeting links

**Recording Without Permission:**


**Anyone can record video calls** using screen recording software—even if the app doesn't show "recording" indicator.


**Assume any video call could be recorded.**


**Before sharing sensitive info:**

- Ask: "Is anyone recording this call?"
- In professional settings: Get consent before recording

**Most platforms show recording indicator:**

- Red dot, "Recording" message
- But this can be bypassed with third-party recording software

**Legal recording requirements vary:**

- Some places require all-party consent (everyone agrees)
- Others require only one-party consent (person recording agrees)
- Know your local laws

**Children on Video Calls:**


**Supervise children's video calls:**

- Ensure they're calling known, trusted people
- Teach them not to share personal information (address, school name, phone number)
- Keep computer in common area (not private bedroom)

**School video calls:**

- Use school-provided platforms with proper safety settings
- Parents can usually observe
- Report any concerning behavior to school immediately

## Conclusion


You've learned:


✅ What video calling is and what you need (device, internet, app)
✅ How to choose the right video calling service for your needs
✅ How to make your first video call step-by-step (FaceTime, WhatsApp, Zoom, Google Meet, Skype)
✅ How to join video calls others send you (clicking links, answering calls)
✅ What all the buttons mean during a call (mute, camera, end, share screen)
✅ How to look and sound your best (lighting, camera position, audio, background)
✅ Video call etiquette (when to mute, how to behave professionally)
✅ How to troubleshoot every common problem (audio, video, connection issues)
✅ How to stay safe and protect your privacy on video calls


**Key Takeaways:**


**Video calling is simpler than it seems:** You join a call, you talk, you see each other. The technology handles the rest. Don't overthink it.


**Start with one service:** FaceTime if you're on Apple devices, WhatsApp or Google Meet otherwise. Master one, then explore others if needed.


**Audio matters more than video:** People tolerate lower video quality but won't tolerate inaudible audio. Prioritize clear sound over perfect video.


**Lighting is everything:** Face a window or lamp. That one change improves video quality more than an expensive camera.


**Mute when not speaking:** Especially in group calls. Single most important etiquette rule.


**Test before important calls:** Five minutes before a job interview or doctor appointment, test your setup with a friend.


**Everyone feels awkward at first:** Looking at yourself on camera feels weird initially. This passes within 2-3 calls. Push through the discomfort—it's temporary.


**You can't break anything:** Worst case scenario in any video call: It doesn't work and you try again. No permanent damage possible. Experiment freely.


**Make your first call today:** Call a patient family member or friend. Tell them you're learning and ask them to help you test everything. That first call removes 90% of the anxiety.


**Video calling connects you to people you love across any distance, at any time, for free. It's one of the most valuable technologies available—and now you know how to use it.** 📹
